title: Hui Min's balloon
stem:
Hui Min fitted a balloon over the mouth of an empty plastic bottle, with the balloon hanging inside. When she blew into the balloon, it inflated only a little.

Which is the best explanation?
key: An "empty" bottle is full of air. Air takes up space, and with no way out it is squashed and pushes back.

options.text: The bottle is empty, so the balloon should fill it. Hui Min did not blow hard enough.
options.pick: The bottle looks empty, so the only thing that could stop the balloon seems to be her blowing.
options.why: The bottle is not empty. It is full of air, and that air takes up the space the balloon needs.

options.text: The bottle already contains air. The air takes up space, and as the balloon grows it squashes that air, which pushes back on the balloon.
options.pick: Ask what is inside the "empty" bottle before Hui Min blows.
options.why: The bottle is full of air, which is matter and takes up space. With the balloon sealing the mouth, that air cannot leave, so it is squashed and pushes back.

options.text: The balloon is too stiff to stretch inside a bottle.
options.pick: Balloons can be hard to blow up, so stiffness seems to be the problem.
options.why: The same balloon inflates easily outside the bottle, or inside a bottle with a hole in it. What stops it is the bottle's air, which cannot get out.

options.text: The air in the bottle is squashed into no space at all, so something else must be stopping the balloon.
options.pick: Air is easy to squash, so it seems it could be squashed out of the way completely.
options.why: Air can be squashed into less space, but never into no space. The more it is squashed, the harder it pushes back.

title: A hole in the base
stem:
Hui Min made a hole in the base of the bottle and blew into the balloon again.

What happened, and why?
key: Give the trapped air a way out, and it leaves to make room.

options.text: The balloon inflated the same amount, because the size of the bottle did not change.
options.pick: The bottle is the same size, so the space for the balloon seems the same.
options.why: The size of the bottle is not what matters. What changed is that the air inside can now leave, so it stops taking up the space the balloon needs.

options.text: Nothing changed, because the bottle was empty before and is still empty.
options.pick: A hole in an empty bottle does not seem to change anything.
options.why: The bottle was never empty: it was full of air. The hole lets that air out, so the balloon inflates much more.

options.text: The balloon inflated more, because air has no mass, so the hole made it disappear.
options.pick: The bottle's air seems to vanish when there is a hole.
options.why: Air does not disappear. It is matter with mass, and it moves out through the hole into the room.

options.text: The balloon inflated much more, because the bottle's air could leave through the hole and make room for it.
options.pick: Think about where the bottle's air can go now.
options.why: As the balloon grows, it pushes the bottle's air out through the hole. The air no longer gets squashed, so it does not push back much.

title: What is matter?
stem:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.

Which of these are all matter?
key: Solids, liquids and gases are all matter. Light and heat are not: they have no mass and take up no space.

options.text: Air, water and sand
options.pick: Check each one: does it have mass, and does it take up space?
options.why: Sand is a solid, water is a liquid and air is a gas. All three have mass and take up space, so all are matter.

options.text: Water and sand only. Air is not matter because you cannot see it.
options.pick: You cannot see or hold air, so it does not seem to count.
options.why: Being invisible does not matter. Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

options.text: Sand only. Water and air have no fixed shape.
options.pick: Only sand keeps its own shape, so only sand seems solid enough to be matter.
options.why: Not having a fixed shape does not stop something being matter. Liquids and gases take the shape of their container, but they still have mass and take up space.

options.text: Light, air and water
options.pick: Light is everywhere around us, like air.
options.why: Light is a form of energy. It has no mass and takes up no space, so it is not matter.

title: Pumping up a football
stem:
Ali measured the mass of a flat football. He then pumped air into it until it was hard, and measured its mass again.

What did he find?
key: Air has mass. Adding air to a ball adds a little mass.

options.text: The mass stayed the same, because air has no mass.
options.pick: Air feels like nothing when you hold it.
options.why: Air is very light, but it is matter and has mass. The extra air adds to the ball's mass.

options.text: The mass decreased, because air makes things lighter.
options.pick: Balloons full of air float about, so air seems to make things lighter.
options.why: Adding matter never makes the total mass smaller. The air adds a little mass.

options.text: The mass increased a little, because air has mass.
options.pick: Air is matter. What does every kind of matter have?
options.why: The air pumped in has mass, so the ball's mass goes up a little.

options.text: The mass stayed the same, because the air only takes up space inside the ball.
options.pick: The air fills the ball out, so it seems to add size, not mass.
options.why: Matter takes up space and has mass. The air does both, so the mass goes up a little.

title: Describing a gas
stem:
The table describes four kinds of matter by their shape and volume.

Which row describes a gas?
key: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume. It spreads out to fill its whole container.

options.pick: Gases have no shape of their own, and their amount seems fixed.
options.why: That describes a liquid. A liquid keeps its volume, but a gas spreads out to fill its container and can be squashed into less space.

options.pick: Think of air in a syringe: it fills the whole space, and you can squash it smaller.
options.why: A gas takes the shape of its container and fills it completely, and it can be compressed, so it has no definite shape or volume.

options.pick: Every material seems to have some shape and some size.
options.why: That describes a solid. A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.

options.pick: It is the only row left that is different from a solid and a liquid.
options.why: No kind of matter keeps its shape but not its volume. A gas has no definite shape either.

title: A sealed syringe of air
stem:
A syringe is filled with air and its nozzle is sealed. The plunger is then pushed in.

Which statement is correct?
key: A gas can be compressed into less space, but it never takes up no space.

options.text: The plunger cannot move at all, because air has a definite volume.
options.pick: The nozzle is sealed, so nothing seems able to move.
options.why: That would be true for water, which has a definite volume. Air is a gas, so it can be squashed into less space.

options.text: The plunger goes all the way in, because the air disappears.
options.pick: Air is easy to squash, so it seems it could be squashed away completely.
options.why: The air cannot disappear or leave the sealed syringe. It is squashed into less space and pushes back harder and harder.

options.text: The plunger goes all the way in, because air takes up no space.
options.pick: Air does not feel like it takes up any room.
options.why: Air is matter, so it takes up space. The trapped air stops the plunger from reaching the end.

options.text: The plunger can be pushed in part of the way, because the air is squashed into less space.
options.pick: Think about whether a gas has a definite volume.
options.why: Air has no definite volume, so it can be compressed into less space. It still takes up space and pushes back, so the plunger cannot go all the way in.

title: A cup pushed into water
stem:
A dry paper towel is stuffed into the bottom of a cup. The cup is turned upside down and pushed straight down into a basin of water. When it is lifted out, the paper towel is still dry.

Why did the paper towel stay dry?
key: The cup is full of air. The trapped air takes up space, so the water cannot fill the cup.

options.text: The cup is empty, so the water has nothing to fill.
options.pick: There seems to be nothing in the cup except the towel.
options.why: The cup is not empty: it is full of air, and that air takes up the space the water would need.

options.text: The air in the cup is squashed into no space, so the water cannot reach the towel.
options.pick: The air gets squashed, so it seems to be pressed away to nothing.
options.why: The air is squashed a little, but it still takes up space. That is exactly what keeps the water away.

options.text: The cup is full of air, which takes up space and keeps the water out.
options.pick: Ask what is inside the "empty" part of the cup.
options.why: The air trapped in the upside-down cup cannot escape, and it takes up space, so water cannot rise up to the towel.

options.text: The paper towel is waterproof.
options.pick: The towel stayed dry, so it seems to be the towel's doing.
options.why: Paper towels absorb water. The towel stayed dry because the trapped air kept the water from reaching it.

title: A funnel sealed into a bottle
stem:
A funnel is fixed tightly into the neck of an empty bottle with modelling clay, so there is no gap. Water poured into the funnel stays in the funnel.

Why does the water stay in the funnel?
key: Air trapped in a sealed bottle takes up space. With no way out, it stops water from coming in.

options.text: The bottle is full of air that cannot escape, so there is no space for the water.
options.pick: Ask what is already in the bottle, and whether it can get out.
options.why: The bottle is full of air. The clay seals it in, so the air cannot leave to make room for the water.

options.text: The funnel must be blocked, because the empty bottle should fill.
options.pick: If the water does not flow, something seems to be stuck in the funnel.
options.why: The funnel is clear. The trapped air in the bottle is what stops the water.

options.text: The clay makes the water stick in the funnel.
options.pick: The clay is the only new thing added, so it seems to be the cause.
options.why: The clay only seals the gap. It is the air sealed inside the bottle that keeps the water out.

options.text: There is nothing in the bottle, so the water has nothing to push against.
options.pick: An empty bottle seems to have nothing in it at all.
options.why: The bottle is full of air, and the air takes up space. That is what the water is stopped by.

title: Two balloons on a balance
stem:
Two identical balloons, both blown up the same amount, hang at the two ends of a balanced stick. One balloon is popped.

What happens to the stick?
key: Air has mass. Losing the air makes that side lighter.

options.text: The stick stays balanced, because air has no mass.
options.pick: Air feels weightless, so losing it seems to change nothing.
options.why: Air is matter and has mass, so losing it does change the balance.

options.text: The side with the popped balloon goes down, because a full balloon is lighter.
options.pick: Balloons full of air seem light and floaty.
options.why: Adding air adds mass. The full balloon is the heavier one.

options.text: The stick stays balanced, because both balloons still have the same rubber.
options.pick: The rubber is the same on both sides, so the mass seems the same.
options.why: The rubber is the same, but only one balloon still has its air, and that air has mass.

options.text: The side with the full balloon goes down, because the air in it has mass.
options.pick: Popping one balloon lets its air out. Does that change the mass on that side?
options.why: The air in the full balloon has mass. The popped side has lost its air, so the full side is now heavier and goes down.

title: A basketball
stem:
A soft basketball with very little air in it has a mass of 560 g. More air is pumped in until the ball is hard.

What could its mass be now?
key: Air has mass, so pumping in air adds a little mass.

options.text: 560 g, because air has no mass
options.pick: Air does not feel like it weighs anything.
options.why: Air is matter, so it has mass. The ball's mass increases a little.

options.text: 565 g, because the extra air has mass
options.pick: Air is matter, so it adds a little mass.
options.why: The air pumped in has mass. It is light, so the mass goes up by only a little.

options.text: 550 g, because air makes the ball lighter
options.pick: A pumped-up ball bounces higher, so it seems lighter.
options.why: Adding matter cannot make the mass smaller. The mass goes up.

options.text: It cannot be measured, because air is not matter.
options.pick: You cannot see the air, so it seems not to count.
options.why: Air is matter: it has mass and takes up space. The balance shows the extra mass.

title: Which is not matter?
stem: Which of the following is not matter?
key: Matter has mass and takes up space. Light and heat do not, so they are not matter.

options.text: Air
options.pick: You cannot see air, so it seems not to be matter.
options.why: Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

options.text: Steam
options.pick: Steam is a gas, and gases seem too thin to count.
options.why: Steam is water as a gas. Gases have mass and take up space, so steam is matter.

options.text: Light
options.pick: Check each one: does it have mass and take up space?
options.why: Light is a form of energy. It has no mass and takes up no space.

options.text: Oxygen
options.pick: Oxygen is invisible, like air.
options.why: Oxygen is a gas. It has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

title: True about matter
key: Matter has mass and takes up space. Heat and light are energy, not matter. A liquid takes the shape of its container.

options.text: Heat is not matter, because it has no mass and takes up no space.
options.pick: Test the statement against the definition of matter.
options.why: Heat is a form of energy. It has no mass and takes up no space, so it is not matter.

options.text: Heat is matter, because you can feel it.
options.pick: Things you can feel seem to be real stuff.
options.why: Being able to feel something does not make it matter. Heat has no mass and takes up no space.

options.text: Water vapour is not matter, because you cannot see it.
options.pick: Invisible things do not seem to be matter.
options.why: Water vapour is a gas. It has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

options.text: A liquid has a definite shape, because it keeps the same shape in a cup.
options.pick: Water in a cup always looks like the cup.
options.why: It looks like the cup because it takes the cup's shape. Pour it into a bowl and its shape changes, so a liquid has no definite shape.

title: Describing a liquid
stem:
The table describes four kinds of matter by their shape and volume.

Which row describes a liquid?
key: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape: it takes the shape of its container.

options.pick: Water in a glass seems to keep its shape.
options.why: That describes a solid. Pour the water into a bowl and its shape changes.

options.pick: Liquids flow everywhere, so they seem to have no fixed anything.
options.why: That describes a gas. A liquid keeps its volume; it cannot be squashed into less space.

options.pick: It is different from both the solid and the gas rows.
options.why: No kind of matter keeps its shape but not its volume. A liquid has a definite volume.

options.pick: Think of 100 mL of water poured from a glass into a bowl.
options.why: It is still 100 mL (definite volume), but it takes the shape of the bowl (no definite shape).

title: What can be squashed?
stem:
Three sealed syringes contain a block of wood, water and air.

In which syringe can the plunger be pushed in?
key: Only a gas can be compressed into less space. Solids and liquids have a definite volume.

options.text: The syringes of air and water
options.pick: Water and air both flow, so both seem squashable.
options.why: Water flows but has a definite volume, so it cannot be squashed into less space.

options.text: Only the syringe of air
options.pick: Which kind of matter has no definite volume?
options.why: Air is a gas with no definite volume, so it can be squashed into less space. Wood and water have definite volumes.

options.text: All three syringes
options.pick: Pushing hard enough seems to squash anything.
options.why: Solids and liquids have a definite volume. Only the gas can be compressed.

options.text: None of them, because nothing can be squashed
options.pick: The syringes are sealed, so nothing seems able to move.
options.why: Air has no definite volume, so it can be compressed even when it is sealed in.

title: Which has mass?
stem: Which of the following has mass and takes up space?
key: Matter has mass and takes up space, even when you cannot see it. Light, heat and sound are energy, not matter.

options.text: The steam from a kettle
options.pick: Look for the one that is made of stuff, even if it is a gas.
options.why: Steam is water as a gas. It has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.

options.text: The light from a torch
options.pick: Light fills a room, so it seems to take up space.
options.why: Light is a form of energy. It has no mass and takes up no space.

options.text: The heat from a fire
options.pick: You can feel heat, so it seems to be something real.
options.why: Heat is a form of energy, not matter. It has no mass and takes up no space.

options.text: The sound of a bell
options.pick: Sound travels through the air and fills a room.
options.why: Sound is a form of energy, not matter. It has no mass.

title: Pumping a bicycle tyre
stem:
A bicycle tyre is already full of air. More air is pumped into it.

Which statement is correct?
key: Air takes up space and has mass. Pumping more in squashes it into less space, and it pushes harder.

options.text: The extra air takes up no space, so the tyre does not get any harder.
options.pick: The tyre hardly changes size, so the extra air seems to take no room.
options.why: The extra air does take up space. It squashes the air already there, which is why the tyre gets harder.

options.text: Air has no mass, so the tyre's mass does not change.
options.pick: Air seems weightless.
options.why: Air has mass. The pumped-up tyre has a slightly greater mass.

options.text: The air inside is squashed into less space and pushes harder on the tyre.
options.pick: The tyre cannot grow much, so think about what happens to the air inside.
options.why: More air in the same space means the air is compressed. Compressed air pushes harder, so the tyre feels harder.

options.text: The tyre was empty until it was pumped up.
options.pick: A flat tyre seems to have nothing in it.
options.why: Even a soft tyre has air in it. Pumping adds more air to what is already there.
